title: Child Penalties Across Countries: Evidence and Explanations
research_question: How does the arrival of the first child affect the labor market trajectories (earnings and employment) of women relative to men, and how does this gendered impact of parenthood vary across countries with different family policies and gender norms? To what extent can government family policies versus prevailing gender norms account for cross-country differences in the long-run earnings consequences of motherhood?
data_description: The study assembles comparable panel data on parents in six countries: Denmark (1980-2013), Sweden (1997-2011), Austria (1980-2017), Germany (SOEP, 1984-2016), the United Kingdom (BHPS, 1991-2009), and the United States (PSID, 1968-present). Scandinavian countries and Austria use full-population administrative registers (social security and income/birth registries), while Germany, the UK, and the US rely on long-running household surveys. Key variables include gross annual labor earnings (before taxes and transfers), employment/participation status, age, calendar year, and the date of birth of the first child, with parents linked to children. The unit of observation is an individual-year. Samples include individuals having their first child between ages 20 and 45, observed from 5 years before to 10 years after first birth. Gender-norm data come from the International Social Survey Programme (ISSP) waves 1988, 1994, 2002, and 2012.
institutional_context: The six countries span a wide range of family-policy regimes and cultural attitudes toward working mothers. Scandinavia (Denmark, Sweden) features extensive public child care and generous, often earmarked, parental leave (including paternity leave in Sweden). The German-speaking countries (Germany, Austria) historically combine long parental leave entitlements with limited public child care for young children and more traditional views about maternal employment. The English-speaking countries (United Kingdom, United States) provide comparatively limited statutory parental leave and rely more on private child care markets. These countries also differ markedly in elicited gender norms, measured by ISSP responses to whether mothers of young or school-age children should stay home rather than work. This cross-country variation in policies, leave durations, child-care availability, and cultural attitudes provides the setting for comparing how the birth of a first child reshapes mothers' versus fathers' careers.
ground_truth_notes: The study uses high-quality panel data and consistent methodology across countries, but cultural and policy differences may introduce unobserved heterogeneity.
